items.title: The Cultural Iceberg
items.text: Imagine an iceberg floating in the sea. Only a small part is visible above the water, while most of it lies hidden below. Many scholars use this picture to explain culture. What we can easily see, such as food, clothing, festivals, and music, is only the tip. Beneath the surface lie invisible things: beliefs about family, ideas of politeness, attitudes toward time, and views on what makes a person successful. These hidden elements shape how people behave, yet members of a culture rarely notice them because they seem natural. Misunderstandings between cultures often begin below the waterline. For example, a visitor may admire a country's colorful dishes but still be puzzled when a host refuses a compliment, not realizing that modesty is highly valued there.

qs.q: What is the passage mainly about?
o: Why food and clothing are the most important parts of any culture
How travelers can avoid every misunderstanding when they go abroad
How the iceberg image explains the visible and hidden sides of culture
Which cultures keep more hidden beliefs than other cultures do around the world
qs.why: 빙산의 비유로 문화의 보이는 부분과 보이지 않는 부분을 설명하는 글이에요.

qs.q: In the passage, the word "shape" is closest in meaning to
o: influence
describe
hide
illustrate
qs.why: hidden elements shape how people behave는 '행동에 영향을 준다'는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: According to the passage, which of the following lies below the surface?
o: Colorful festivals
Traditional folk music
Everyday clothing
Attitudes toward time
qs.why: 시간에 대한 태도는 보이지 않는 부분으로 언급돼요. 나머지는 빙산의 윗부분(tip)이에요.

qs.q: Why do members of a culture rarely notice the hidden elements?
o: Those ideas are kept secret by older people.
Those ideas feel natural to them.
Those ideas change every single year.
Those ideas are taught only to visitors.
qs.why: because they seem natural에서 알 수 있어요.

qs.q: Why does the writer mention a host who refuses a compliment?
o: To prove that modesty is a weakness in most places
To show how a hidden value can cause confusion
To explain why visitors dislike unfamiliar dishes
To argue that compliments should always be avoided
qs.why: 겸손이라는 숨은 가치관이 오해를 낳는 예로 쓰였어요.

items.title: Hello in Many Ways
items.text: A greeting seems like the simplest part of social life, yet it can be a source of surprise. In some countries, people shake hands firmly and look directly at each other. In others, a gentle bow shows respect, and the depth of the bow may depend on age or position. Some communities greet friends with a kiss on the cheek, and in a few places people touch noses or place a hand on the heart. Travelers often worry about doing the wrong thing, but most hosts are forgiving when a visitor makes an honest effort. A useful strategy is to watch what local people do first and then follow their lead. If you are still unsure, a warm smile and a simple "hello" in the local language are rarely a mistake.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the main point of the passage?
o: Handshakes are the only polite greeting in the whole modern world today.
Bowing has replaced kissing in most communities today.
Travelers should avoid greeting strangers in foreign places.
Greetings differ widely, so observing locals is a wise approach.
qs.why: 다양한 인사 방식을 소개하고 현지인을 관찰하라는 조언으로 끝나요.

qs.q: What can be inferred about hosts who meet foreign visitors?
o: They usually appreciate sincere attempts to follow local customs.
They expect visitors to know every local greeting perfectly.
They feel deeply insulted whenever a visitor makes a small mistake.
They prefer visitors who never try the local language.
qs.why: most hosts are forgiving when a visitor makes an honest effort에서 추론할 수 있어요.

qs.q: According to the passage, the depth of a bow may depend on
o: the season of the year
the language spoken
the age or position of the people
the season of the year and weather
qs.why: the depth of the bow may depend on age or position.

qs.q: What does "follow their lead" most likely mean?
o: walk in front of local people
ask local people for money
teach local people your habits
copy what local people do
qs.why: follow someone's lead는 '그 사람이 하는 대로 따라 하다'라는 뜻이에요.

items.title: The Meaning of a Gift
items.text: Choosing a gift for a host abroad can be harder than it looks. In some places, guests are expected to open a present immediately and show delight in front of the giver. In others, opening it at once would seem greedy, so the gift is set aside until the guest has left. Even small details carry meaning. A certain color of wrapping paper may suggest celebration in one culture and sadness in another, and the number of items in a set may be thought lucky or unlucky. Because of this, many experienced travelers ask a local friend for advice before buying anything. The aim is not to follow a rigid rulebook but to show that you have thought about the other person's feelings, which is what a gift is really meant to say.

qs.q: What is the main message of the passage?
o: Expensive presents are always better than simple ones.
A gift should show care for the receiver's own customs and feelings.
Every culture in the world follows exactly the same gift rules every time.
Travelers should stop bringing gifts to their hosts.
qs.why: 마지막 문장에서 선물의 진짜 의미는 상대방의 감정을 배려하는 것이라고 말해요.

qs.q: According to the passage, why might a guest NOT open a gift at once?
o: Doing so could look greedy in some cultures.
The wrapping paper is usually too expensive to tear.
The host would have no time to enjoy the present.
The gift is meant to be shared with strangers.
qs.why: opening it at once would seem greedy.

qs.q: The word "rigid" in the passage is closest in meaning to
o: short and simple
old and extremely valuable
strict and unchangeable
old and valuable
qs.why: rigid rulebook은 '엄격하고 융통성 없는 규칙집'이라는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: What does the writer suggest experienced travelers do before buying a gift?
o: Get advice from someone who knows the local culture
Search for the cheapest possible gift in the local market
Choose a set with the largest number of items
Wrap the present in their favorite color
qs.why: many experienced travelers ask a local friend for advice.

qs.q: What can be inferred from the sentence about wrapping paper?
o: Paper of any color is rarely used for wrapping gifts anywhere.
Sadness is the main purpose of wrapping a gift.
Colors do not carry the same meaning everywhere.
People in all cultures prefer the same color.
qs.why: 같은 색이 문화에 따라 축하 또는 슬픔을 뜻할 수 있다고 했어요.

items.title: What Time Does Dinner Start?
items.text: Researchers who study time sometimes divide cultures into two broad types. In one, people tend to do a single task at a time, follow schedules closely, and consider arriving late a sign of disrespect. In the other, relationships matter more than the clock, several things may happen at once, and a meeting can start when everyone has finally arrived. Neither style is better; each works well in its own setting. Problems appear when the two meet. A manager used to strict schedules may think a late colleague is careless, while the colleague may think the manager is cold and impatient. Understanding that both people are acting on reasonable assumptions makes it easier to be patient and to find a middle path, such as agreeing on a start time and a flexible finish.

qs.q: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How managers can make their late colleagues arrive much earlier
Two different approaches to time and the conflicts they can cause
Why strict schedules are better than flexible ones
The history of clocks in different societies
qs.why: 시간에 대한 두 가지 관점과 그 충돌을 다뤄요.

qs.q: What does the writer say about the two styles of time?
o: The first is clearly more modern than the second.
The second is the reason why meetings fail.
Both disappeared when people began to travel.
Each is effective in its own context.
qs.why: Neither style is better; each works well in its own setting.

qs.q: In the second type of culture, a meeting may begin
o: exactly at the planned minute
only when the manager decides
after all the people have arrived
before anybody comes into the room
qs.why: a meeting can start when everyone has finally arrived.

qs.q: Which situation is the best example of the problem described in the passage?
o: A punctual manager thinks a relaxed colleague does not care.
Two managers agree to start at nine o'clock and both come early.
A colleague forgets a meeting because of heavy snow.
A student asks for extra time to finish the homework.
qs.why: 서로 다른 시간관이 만나 오해가 생기는 예예요.

qs.q: Which solution does the writer suggest?
o: Ban every meeting that lasts for more than an hour
Ask the late colleague to leave the company
Let each person arrive at any moment they wish
Fix a start time but allow a flexible ending
qs.why: such as agreeing on a start time and a flexible finish.

items.title: Standing Close, Looking Away
items.text: Every person carries an invisible bubble of personal space, but its size changes from one culture to another. In some societies, friends chat at arm's length and a closer step feels pushy. In others, people stand much nearer, and moving back may look like coldness. Eye contact works in a similar way. Many English speakers regard steady eye contact as a sign of honesty and interest. In other cultures, however, looking directly at an older person or a teacher may be considered impolite, so students lower their eyes to show respect. These habits are learned in childhood and rarely discussed, which is why they can create awkward moments between strangers. Instead of judging the other person quickly, it helps to ask whether the behavior simply follows a different set of unwritten rules.

qs.q: What is the writer's attitude toward differences in personal space and eye contact?
o: Critical, strict and impatient
Understanding and open-minded
Amused and careless
Doubtful and fearful
qs.why: 상대를 빨리 판단하기보다 다른 규칙일 수 있다고 열린 태도를 권해요.

qs.q: According to the passage, why might a student avoid looking directly at a teacher?
o: The teacher usually asks students to look away.
It can be seen as a lack of respect in some cultures.
Eye contact is difficult for people who speak English.
Students are afraid of becoming too honest.
qs.why: looking directly at an older person or a teacher may be considered impolite.

qs.q: The phrase "pushy" in the passage most likely means
o: quietly friendly
pleasantly generous toward others
slightly confused
too forceful toward others
qs.why: a closer step feels pushy는 '밀어붙이는 듯 불편하다'는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: Why can these habits cause awkward moments between strangers?
o: Nobody has ever clearly explained them to us.
Strangers usually refuse to speak to each other.
They only appear when people are adults.
They are written in different languages.
qs.why: learned in childhood and rarely discussed.

items.title: One Language, Many Englishes
items.text: English is no longer the property of a few countries. Roughly speaking, there are three groups of speakers. In some countries, English is the first language of most people. In others, such as India or Nigeria, it is an additional language used in schools, courts, and government, and it has developed its own vocabulary and rhythm. In a third group, which includes Korea, English is studied as a foreign language and used mainly to communicate with outsiders. Because the second and third groups together are far larger than the first, most conversations in English today do not include a native speaker at all. For this reason, many teachers argue that clear and polite communication matters more than copying one particular accent, and that learners should be ready to understand a range of varieties.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: English should be taught only by native speakers from a few large countries.
Only three countries still teach English in school.
English has several varieties and is used among many kinds of speakers.
Accents are the most important part of language study.
qs.why: 영어를 쓰는 사람의 세 가지 유형과 다양한 영어를 다뤄요.

qs.q: According to the passage, how is English used in countries like India or Nigeria?
o: As a language that nobody studies in school
As the only language of every home
As a hobby for travelers
As an extra language in public life
qs.why: an additional language used in schools, courts, and government.

qs.q: What does the writer imply about conversations in English today?
o: Most of them are held in English-speaking countries.
Most of them take place without any native speaker.
Most of them are about school subjects.
Most of them are shorter than a minute.
qs.why: most conversations in English today do not include a native speaker at all.

qs.q: What do many teachers believe, according to the passage?
o: Clarity and politeness are more valuable than a perfect accent.
Learners should copy one accent as closely as possible.
Understanding other varieties is not necessary for English learners today.
Grammar is less important than pronunciation.
qs.why: clear and polite communication matters more than copying one particular accent.

qs.q: The word "range" in the last sentence is closest in meaning to
o: limit
rule
variety
distance
qs.why: a range of varieties는 '다양한 종류'라는 뜻이에요.

items.title: Words That Travelled
items.text: The English dictionary is full of travelers. The word "safari" arrived from Swahili, where it simply means a journey. "Pajamas" came through languages of South Asia, and "tsunami" was borrowed from Japanese, where it describes a powerful sea wave. Ketchup is thought to have started as a fish sauce in southern China before European sailors carried the idea home and changed the recipe. When a word moves, its meaning often shifts. "Safari" now suggests a trip to see wild animals, a narrower idea than the original. Borrowing is not a sign of weakness in a language; it shows that people have met, traded, and learned from one another. Studying where words come from can therefore be a small history lesson about how cultures have been connected for centuries.

qs.q: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How borrowed words show contact between cultures
Why English is a weaker language than Swahili
How to prepare for a trip to see wild animals
Which foods are the most popular around the world
qs.why: 외래어가 문화 간 접촉을 보여 준다는 내용이에요.

qs.q: Which statement about "safari" is supported by the passage?
o: It was originally a word for a sea wave.
It is borrowed from a language of South Asia.
Its meaning has become narrower in English.
It no longer has anything to do with travel.
qs.why: 원래는 단순한 '여행'이었지만 지금은 야생동물 여행을 가리켜요.

qs.q: What does the writer think about borrowing words?
o: It damages a language over time.
It reflects people learning from one another.
It happens only in very small languages.
It should be avoided in all modern dictionaries and textbooks.
qs.why: Borrowing is not a sign of weakness ... it shows that people have met, traded, and learned.

qs.q: According to the passage, which word is connected with the sea?
o: pajamas
safari
dictionary
tsunami
qs.why: tsunami는 '강력한 바다 파도'를 뜻해요.

items.title: A Cup of Tea
items.text: Few drinks cross borders as easily as tea, yet each place has made it its own. In some countries, tea is brewed strong, mixed with milk, and enjoyed with a small snack in the afternoon. In others, a small cup of clear green tea is sipped slowly after a meal, and preparing it for guests can follow careful steps that have been practiced for generations. Elsewhere, tea is poured from a height into tiny glasses, sweetened, and offered again and again as a sign of welcome. What links these customs is not the leaf itself but the idea of sharing time. A cup of tea says, "Sit down for a moment." Even when the recipe and the cup change, the message that people want to connect remains much the same.

qs.q: What do the different tea customs have in common?
o: They all use exactly the same kind of leaf.
They all take place in the afternoon.
They all express a wish to spend time together.
They all require expensive equipment from a specialist shop.
qs.why: What links these customs is ... the idea of sharing time.

qs.q: The writer mentions pouring tea from a height in order to
o: give an example of a distinct way of serving tea
prove that tea always tastes better in tiny glasses
warn readers about burning their hands
explain why green tea is sweet
qs.why: 다양한 차 문화의 한 사례로 소개됐어요.

qs.q: What is the purpose of the sentence "Sit down for a moment"?
o: To give readers an order from the writer
To describe a rule of the tea ceremony
To tell travelers to leave a restaurant
To show what a cup of tea communicates
qs.why: 차 한 잔이 전하는 메시지를 표현한 문장이에요.

qs.q: Which title best fits the passage?
o: How to Grow the Best Tea Leaves
One Drink, Many Ways of Welcoming
The Rise and Fall of Afternoon Snacks
Why Milk Does Not Belong in Tea
qs.why: 차를 통한 환대와 교류의 다양한 방식이 중심이에요.

items.title: When Cuisines Meet
items.text: Walk through a large city and you may find a taco filled with Korean-style beef, a pizza topped with sweet potato, or a burger served with a spicy sauce from another continent. This blending of food traditions is often called fusion cuisine. Supporters say that it shows creativity and helps people to taste unfamiliar flavors in a comfortable way. Critics, however, worry that mixing everything together may hide the history behind a traditional dish, or that a restaurant may use a famous name without understanding its origin. A thoughtful chef therefore tries to learn how a dish is made and why it matters to the community that created it. When this respect is present, fusion can become a delicious form of conversation rather than a careless copy.

qs.q: What is the writer's view of fusion cuisine?
o: It is always harmful to traditional food and to local communities in cities.
It can be valuable if the chef shows respect for the original dish.
It is only a passing fashion in large cities.
It is easier to cook than traditional food.
qs.why: 존중이 있을 때 fusion은 좋은 대화가 될 수 있다고 해요.

qs.q: According to the passage, what do critics worry about?
o: Fusion dishes are too expensive for most people.
Chefs refuse to use any spicy sauce.
Restaurants in large cities close too early.
The history of a dish might be forgotten.
qs.why: mixing everything together may hide the history behind a traditional dish.

qs.q: The phrase "a careless copy" refers to
o: borrowing a dish without understanding it
a photograph of a menu
a very cheap restaurant near the railway station
a recipe written down twice
qs.why: careless copy는 이해 없이 흉내만 내는 것을 뜻해요.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as an example of fusion?
o: A taco with Korean-style beef
A pizza with sweet potato
A soup served with rice and vegetables
A burger served with a spicy sauce from abroad
qs.why: 수프 예는 지문에 없어요.

items.title: Lost in Translation
items.text: Anyone who has translated word for word knows how strange the result can be. If a Korean speaker says "I have a wide face" to mean that they know many people, an English speaker may simply picture a wide face. English has its own puzzling expressions: "break a leg" is good wishes before a performance, and "it's a piece of cake" means that something is easy. Learners who translate such phrases literally may be confused or even amused. The solution is not to avoid idioms but to meet them in context, notice the situation in which they appear, and practice using them. Over time, the pictures that once seemed odd begin to feel natural, and the learner starts to see how each language turns everyday experience into colorful images.

qs.q: What problem does the passage point out?
o: Idioms are used only by young people.
English has no expressions that are used to wish people good luck.
Korean and English have the same idioms.
Literal translation of expressions can confuse listeners.
qs.why: 관용 표현을 직역하면 의미가 전달되지 않을 수 있어요.

qs.q: What does "break a leg" mean in the passage?
o: A warning about a dangerous stage
Good luck before a performance
A request to stop the show
A medical problem of an actor
qs.why: break a leg is good wishes before a performance.

qs.q: What solution does the writer recommend?
o: Meet idioms in real situations and use them
Avoid all idioms until one is an expert
Memorize a list of idioms in alphabetical order
Translate each word with a dictionary
qs.why: meet them in context ... and practice using them.

qs.q: Why does the writer say the learner's feelings about idioms change over time?
o: Idioms are slowly replaced by simple words.
Teachers stop correcting the learner's mistakes.
Familiar use makes strange images feel natural.
Native speakers use fewer idioms with learners.
qs.why: Over time, the pictures that once seemed odd begin to feel natural.

qs.q: The word "amused" is closest in meaning to
o: entertained
worried
disappointed
exhausted
qs.why: amused는 '재미있어하는'이라는 뜻이에요.

items.title: Who Cleans the Classroom?
items.text: In many schools around the world, a team of workers cleans the classrooms after the students go home. In some Japanese schools, however, students themselves sweep the floors, wipe the desks, and clean the corridors every day. Teachers explain that the practice is part of education, not a punishment. Children learn to look after shared spaces, to cooperate in small groups, and to feel grateful to those who work behind the scenes. Visitors from other countries are often surprised, and some wonder whether the time could be spent studying. Yet supporters reply that the habits learned while holding a broom stay with students long after they have forgotten a math formula. The example shows that schools reflect a society's beliefs about what young people ought to learn, not just what is written in textbooks.

qs.q: What is the main point of the passage?
o: Students in all countries must clean their own classrooms.
Cleaning is the best way to punish students.
Daily school routines can reveal what a society values.
Math formulas are more useful than manners.
qs.why: 청소 관행을 통해 사회의 가치관이 학교에 반영됨을 보여 줘요.

qs.q: According to the teachers, the cleaning practice is
o: a kind of punishment
a form of education
a way to save money
a contest between classes
qs.why: the practice is part of education, not a punishment.

qs.q: Which skill is NOT mentioned as something students learn from cleaning?
o: Caring for shared spaces
Working together in small groups
Being thankful to people behind the scenes
Speaking in public
qs.why: 공개 연설은 언급되지 않았어요.

qs.q: What does the phrase "stay with students" suggest?
o: The students refuse to go home.
The classrooms remain dirty.
The habits are remembered for many years.
The teachers follow the students everywhere.
qs.why: 습관이 오랫동안 남는다는 뜻이에요.

items.title: Guests and Hosts
items.text: In many parts of the world, hospitality is treated as a serious duty. A host may offer food and drink several times, and a guest is expected to refuse politely at first before accepting. For a visitor from a place where a "no" is taken at face value, this can be confusing: if you say you are full, you may find another plate in front of you. Understanding the custom changes everything. The host is not ignoring your wishes; the repeated offer is a way of showing that the invitation is sincere. The visitor, in turn, can accept a small portion, praise the cooking, and explain kindly if it is truly impossible to eat more. In this way both sides show respect, even though they use different signals.

qs.q: Why might a host offer food again after a guest says no?
o: The repeated offer shows that the invitation is sincere.
The host did not clearly hear the guest's answer the first time.
The host wants the guest to leave sooner.
The host believes the food is too expensive.
qs.why: the repeated offer is a way of showing that the invitation is sincere.

qs.q: What is a suitable response for a visitor who cannot eat more?
o: Leave the table without saying anything
Say politely that the food is not very tasty
Eat everything even if feeling unwell
Accept a small portion and explain kindly
qs.why: accept a small portion, praise the cooking, and explain kindly.

qs.q: What does "taken at face value" mean in this passage?
o: decided after a very long discussion
understood exactly as it is said
paid for with a small coin
answered with a smile
qs.why: at face value는 '말 그대로 받아들여지다'라는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: What can be concluded from the passage?
o: Hosts should never offer food twice.
Different signals can express the same respect.
Guests should always eat everything that is served to them.
Visitors cannot learn foreign customs.
qs.why: both sides show respect, even though they use different signals.

items.title: Voices of the Griot
items.text: Long before books were common, many communities kept their history alive by speaking it aloud. In parts of West Africa, specially trained storytellers known as griots remembered family histories, important events, and songs, and performed them at weddings and ceremonies. A griot did more than entertain. By recalling the achievements of ancestors, the storyteller reminded listeners of the values that held the community together. Memory was a skill taught over many years, and audiences often took part by answering or clapping. Today, written records are easy to store, but oral traditions have not disappeared. Grandparents who tell family stories, or a poet who recites a poem on stage, continue the same ancient idea: that a story told face to face can carry feelings that a printed page may not.

qs.q: What role did griots play in their communities?
o: They wrote the first printed books in the whole region of Africa.
They collected taxes from the families nearby.
They trained farmers in new skills.
They kept history and shared values through spoken stories.
qs.why: 역사를 기억하고 구술로 가치를 전했어요.

qs.q: According to the passage, how did audiences often take part?
o: By answering or clapping
By writing notes on paper
By paying with food
By staying silent
qs.why: audiences often took part by answering or clapping.

qs.q: What does the writer imply about oral traditions today?
o: They have been replaced entirely by books.
They are practiced only in West Africa.
They still exist in modern forms.
They are considered less valuable than before.
qs.why: Grandparents who tell family stories ... continue the same idea.

qs.q: The word "recalling" in the passage is closest in meaning to
o: inventing
forgetting
questioning
remembering
qs.why: recalling은 '기억해 내다'라는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: Which statement would the writer most likely agree with?
o: Spoken stories are always more accurate than written ones.
Face-to-face storytelling can convey feelings in a special way.
Poetry should be read only silently by each person alone at home.
Memory is no longer a useful skill.
qs.why: a story told face to face can carry feelings that a printed page may not.

items.title: Why Stereotypes Fail
items.text: A stereotype is a simple idea about a group of people that is applied to every member of that group. Some stereotypes sound harmless, even positive, such as "people from that country are always polite," yet they are still problematic. They ignore the fact that individuals differ, and they can pressure people to act in a fixed way. Psychologists explain that the brain likes shortcuts, so it quickly sorts new people into categories. The danger lies in stopping there. A useful alternative is a generalization that is held loosely: it describes a common tendency but remains open to exceptions. Meeting people personally, reading a variety of sources, and asking questions all help to replace a fixed picture with a more accurate and more respectful one.

qs.q: According to the passage, why can even positive stereotypes be a problem?
o: They treat all members of a group as if they were the same.
They make people lose all of their interest in travel abroad.
They are mostly invented by psychologists.
They are spread only through television.
qs.why: They ignore the fact that individuals differ.

qs.q: What is the difference between a stereotype and a loose generalization?
o: A stereotype is always based on scientific facts.
A generalization applies to every single person.
A generalization stays open to exceptions.
A stereotype describes only one individual.
qs.why: a generalization ... remains open to exceptions.

qs.q: The writer mentions the brain's liking for shortcuts in order to
o: explain why people sort others into categories
prove that stereotypes are always accurate and useful
show that psychologists dislike travel
argue that learning is impossible
qs.why: the brain likes shortcuts, so it quickly sorts new people into categories.

qs.q: Which of the following is suggested as a way to reduce stereotypes?
o: Avoiding all contact with foreigners
Trusting the first impression
Reading from many different sources
Using only one news website
qs.why: reading a variety of sources.

items.title: The Curve of Culture Shock
items.text: Moving to a new country is often described as a curve with ups and downs. At first, many people feel excited; everything is new, and small differences seem charming. After some weeks, the mood can change. Simple tasks such as buying food or taking a bus become tiring, and homesickness grows. This low point is commonly called culture shock. It is not a sign of weakness but a natural reaction to the stress of living without familiar signals. With time, newcomers learn local habits, make friends, and find routines that bring comfort. Eventually many people reach a stage of balance, in which they can enjoy both their old and new surroundings. Knowing that the curve is normal helps people to be patient with themselves during the difficult part.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the passage?
o: To advise readers never to move abroad for their studies or work
To explain that culture shock is a normal stage of adjustment
To compare food in different countries
To list the reasons why people feel excited
qs.why: 문화 충격이 적응 과정의 자연스러운 단계임을 설명해요.

qs.q: According to the passage, when does culture shock usually begin?
o: Before the traveler leaves home for a trip
On the very first day of the trip
After the person has returned home
After the first excitement has faded
qs.why: 처음의 흥분 뒤, 몇 주 후에 기분이 변해요.

qs.q: What does the writer say about culture shock?
o: It happens only to careless people.
It lasts for exactly one year.
It is a natural response to stress.
It can be avoided by staying in a hotel.
qs.why: It is not a sign of weakness but a natural reaction.

qs.q: Which stage is described last in the passage?
o: A balance between old and new surroundings
Excitement about many new and unusual things
Tiredness from ordinary tasks
Homesickness for friends
qs.why: 마지막 단계는 두 환경을 모두 즐기는 균형이에요.

qs.q: The word "charming" in the passage is closest in meaning to
o: dangerous and extremely loud
boring and plain
expensive and heavy
pleasant and attractive
qs.why: charming은 '매력적인'이라는 뜻이에요.

items.title: Words Without Borders
items.text: Some words seem to hold an entire way of life. The Danish word "hygge" describes a cozy feeling of comfort created by candles, warm drinks, and good company. The Portuguese "saudade" is a tender longing for someone or something that is absent. In Japanese, "komorebi" names the sunlight that filters through the leaves of trees. English speakers can describe each of these ideas, but only with a phrase or a sentence, which suggests that their own language never needed a single word for them. Linguists are careful here: having no word does not mean that people cannot feel or notice something. Still, a word makes an idea easier to share and remember, so learning such terms is a gentle way to see what different communities pay attention to.

qs.q: What does the writer say about languages that lack a single word for an idea?
o: Speakers are completely unable to feel or notice the idea.
Speakers can still notice and explain the idea.
Speakers must borrow the word immediately.
Speakers have not met anyone who feels it.
qs.why: having no word does not mean that people cannot feel or notice something.

qs.q: Which word describes sunlight passing through leaves?
o: etiquette
komorebi
saudade
safari
qs.why: komorebi는 나뭇잎 사이로 스며드는 햇빛을 뜻해요.

qs.q: What is the purpose of the last sentence?
o: To warn readers about difficult pronunciation
To claim that English is a limited language
To end the discussion about Portuguese
To suggest a benefit of learning such words
qs.why: 그런 단어를 배우면 공동체가 무엇에 주목하는지 알 수 있다고 해요.

qs.q: The word "tender" in the passage is closest in meaning to
o: gentle
harsh
sudden
silent
qs.why: tender longing은 '애틋한 그리움'이에요.

items.title: Houses That Fit Their Places
items.text: The shape of a home often tells a story about the land and the people who built it. In regions with heavy seasonal floods, houses are lifted on tall posts so that water flows beneath them. In hot, dry areas, thick walls and small windows keep rooms cool, and an inner courtyard offers shade and a private place for the family. In cold northern lands, steep roofs allow snow to slide off, while small rooms are easier to heat. But climate is not the only factor. Beliefs about family can shape a house too: some designs gather several generations under one roof, whereas others prefer separate rooms for privacy. By reading a building carefully, a visitor can guess something about both the weather and the values of a community.

qs.q: Why are houses in flood-prone regions built on tall posts?
o: So that people can see the stars
So that snow slides off the roof
So that water can pass underneath
So that the rooms stay warm in winter
qs.why: houses are lifted on tall posts so that water flows beneath them.

qs.q: According to the passage, what is the purpose of thick walls in hot, dry areas?
o: To block the noise of visitors
To store water for the winter
To make the building look old
To keep the rooms cool
qs.why: thick walls and small windows keep rooms cool.

qs.q: What does the word "whereas" show in the passage?
o: A reason for choosing the design
A contrast between two designs
A time sequence
A repeated example
qs.why: whereas는 대조를 나타내요.

qs.q: What can be inferred from the final sentence?
o: Buildings reflect both nature and social values.
Visitors cannot learn anything useful from old buildings.
Climate alone decides how a house looks.
Modern houses are always bigger than old ones.
qs.why: 날씨와 공동체의 가치관을 모두 읽을 수 있다고 해요.

items.title: More Than a Game
items.text: Sports can look like simple entertainment, but they often carry cultural messages. In some societies, team sports such as football or volleyball are especially popular, and success is celebrated as a victory for the whole group. In others, individual achievements are highlighted, and the champion is treated as a hero who has overcome personal challenges. Traditional games reveal values too. A game that requires players to keep a ball in the air using only their feet and heads needs cooperation, balance, and trust. Even the way fans behave, whether they sing together, sit quietly, or applaud both teams, shows what a community expects from spectators. Watching a sport from another culture can therefore be an enjoyable first step toward understanding how people prefer to compete and to celebrate together.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Team sports are always better than individual sports.
Champions should not be celebrated.
Sports can reflect the values of a culture.
Fans should always sing together.
qs.why: 스포츠가 문화적 메시지와 가치를 담고 있다는 내용이에요.

qs.q: According to the passage, what does a game played with feet and heads require?
o: Cooperation, balance, and trust
Speed, strength, and long practice
Expensive equipment
A very large field
qs.why: needs cooperation, balance, and trust.

qs.q: What do the fans' behaviors indicate?
o: Which team is more skilful than the others
How old the stadium is
What a community expects from spectators
Whether the game is fair
qs.why: the way fans behave shows what a community expects from spectators.

qs.q: Which is true about individual achievements, according to the passage?
o: They are ignored in every culture around the whole world.
In some societies the champion is regarded as a hero.
They are less important than the weather.
They are celebrated only in team sports.
qs.why: the champion is treated as a hero.

qs.q: The word "spectators" is closest in meaning to
o: people who play a game
people who sell tickets
people who build stadiums
people who watch an event
qs.why: spectator는 '관중'이에요.

items.title: Bringing a Language Back
items.text: When a language is no longer passed from parents to children, it may disappear within a few generations. Around the world, thousands of languages are in danger, and with each loss a community may lose songs, stories, and ways of describing nature. Yet recovery is possible. In Wales, the local language declined during the twentieth century, but families, schools, and broadcasters worked together to restore it. Children now study in Welsh-medium classes, road signs appear in two languages, and young musicians write modern songs in the old tongue. The effort shows that a language survives when it is useful and valued in daily life, not only in a museum. Technology also helps, as apps and online dictionaries let learners practice wherever they live.

qs.q: According to the passage, what is lost when a language disappears?
o: Only a long list of words and grammar rules
The ability to learn other languages
Stories and ways of describing the world
The history of schools
qs.why: songs, stories, and ways of describing nature.

qs.q: Which factor helped Welsh to recover?
o: Cooperation among families, schools, and broadcasters
A ban on all foreign music and foreign television programs
A rule that road signs must be removed
The closing of all libraries
qs.why: families, schools, and broadcasters worked together.

qs.q: What does the writer mean by "not only in a museum"?
o: A museum has no use for any kind of language.
Old words are never displayed.
Learners should visit museums daily.
A language must be used in everyday life.
qs.why: 언어가 살아남으려면 일상에서 쓰여야 한다는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: What role does technology play in the passage?
o: It makes minority languages totally unnecessary today.
It gives learners more places to practice.
It replaces teachers completely.
It is blamed for language loss.
qs.why: apps and online dictionaries let learners practice wherever they live.

items.title: Meal Times Around the Clock
items.text: When a traveler arrives in a new country, the stomach may be the first part of the body to feel confused. In some places, the main meal is eaten at noon, and shops close for several hours so that families can eat together and rest. In other places, lunch is quick and light, and a large dinner is served late in the evening. Some regions have a mid-afternoon snack that is almost a meal in itself. These patterns grew out of climate, farm work, and the hours of daily life. For example, a break during the hottest part of the day makes sense where the sun is strong. With changing work habits, some of these traditions are fading, but many people still protect them as a way to keep family life from being rushed.

qs.q: Why does a long midday break make sense in some regions?
o: The farms are always closed on that day.
The sun is strongest during that time.
Shops want to avoid selling food.
People are forbidden to work after noon.
qs.why: a break during the hottest part of the day makes sense where the sun is strong.

qs.q: What does the passage say about meal patterns?
o: They were designed by modern restaurants and hotels.
They are the same in every country.
They have never changed.
They developed from climate and work life.
qs.why: These patterns grew out of climate, farm work, and the hours of daily life.

qs.q: What is the writer's attitude toward traditional meal times?
o: Respectful of their value for family life
Convinced that they are completely old-fashioned
Worried that they cost too much
Surprised that anyone remembers them
qs.why: many people still protect them as a way to keep family life from being rushed.

qs.q: The phrase "fading" in the passage is closest in meaning to
o: quickly growing
suddenly changing
slowly disappearing
carefully recording
qs.why: fade는 '서서히 사라지다'예요.

items.title: Please Wait Your Turn
items.text: Public places are full of unspoken rules. In some countries, people form a neat line at a bus stop, and pushing ahead is considered a serious offense. In others, the crowd gathers around the door, and each person finds a gap when the bus arrives. Neither habit is wrong, but visitors can be shocked by the unfamiliar one. Rules about noise differ as well. On some trains, passengers speak quietly or not at all, and a phone call would draw angry looks, while elsewhere lively conversation among strangers is a pleasant part of the trip. Because these rules are rarely printed on signs, newcomers learn them by watching. A simple habit, such as noticing how loudly other passengers talk, can save a visitor from embarrassment and show consideration for the people nearby.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Lines at bus stops are required by law in every country today.
Trains should be completely silent.
Strangers must never talk in public.
Unwritten rules for public behavior vary from place to place.
qs.why: 공공장소의 암묵적 규칙이 문화마다 다름을 말해요.

qs.q: According to the passage, how do newcomers usually learn the rules?
o: By reading printed signs
By watching other people
By attending lessons
By asking the driver
qs.why: newcomers learn them by watching.

qs.q: What does the writer imply about the two ways of boarding a bus?
o: Neither is automatically better.
The first is much quicker than the second.
The second is forbidden in most cities.
Both are becoming impossible.
qs.why: Neither habit is wrong.

qs.q: The word "consideration" in the passage is closest in meaning to
o: a decision about price
a reward for work
thoughtfulness for others
a quick argument between neighbors
qs.why: consideration은 '배려'예요.

items.title: Singing in Two Languages
items.text: Walk into a music shop today and you will notice songs that mix languages. A chorus in English may follow a verse in Korean, Spanish, or Hindi. Producers say that English phrases are easy for listeners around the world to remember, while the local language keeps the song close to the singer's own identity. Some critics worry that global hits might make all music sound alike. Others point out that listeners are also curious: a fan who enjoys a foreign song often searches for the meaning of the lyrics, discovers new customs, and even begins to learn the language. In this sense, pop music can serve as an open door. It does not replace local traditions, but it invites more people to stand at the threshold and look inside.

qs.q: Why do producers include English phrases in songs, according to the passage?
o: They are easy for a worldwide audience to remember.
They are much cheaper to record than local words are.
They are required by music shops.
They always improve the melody.
qs.why: English phrases are easy for listeners around the world to remember.

qs.q: What concern do some critics have?
o: Singers will refuse to use any English.
Local songs will be sold at much lower prices in shops.
Music around the world may start to sound similar.
Fans will stop buying albums.
qs.why: global hits might make all music sound alike.

qs.q: What does "an open door" represent?
o: A fee that people pay for entering a concert hall
A way to enter and explore another culture
A rule that restricts lyrics
A device that records sound
qs.why: pop music can serve as an open door는 다른 문화를 접하는 통로를 뜻해요.

qs.q: Which of the following can be inferred about fans of foreign songs?
o: All of them can read the original lyrics at once without help.
Most of them dislike local traditions.
None of them search for information.
Some of them become interested in learning the language.
qs.why: even begins to learn the language.

qs.q: The word "threshold" is closest in meaning to
o: staircase
window
entrance
floor
qs.why: threshold는 문턱, 즉 '입구'예요.

items.title: A Smile Is Not a Gesture
items.text: Scientists who study emotion have found that some facial expressions are recognized almost everywhere. A person who smiles with real pleasure or frowns in anger is usually understood, even across large cultural gaps. Hand gestures, on the other hand, are much more local. A thumbs-up sign may mean "good job" in one place, but it can be rude elsewhere. A wave that says "come here" in one region might say "go away" in another. Because gestures feel natural to the person who makes them, it is easy to forget that they are learned. A traveler who is unsure should rely more on words, a calm voice, and a friendly face, and avoid gestures unless he or she has checked their meaning. This distinction between what is shared and what is local helps explain both our common humanity and our differences.

qs.q: What is the main contrast in the passage?
o: Facial expressions are widely shared, but gestures are often local.
Smiles are rude in every country, while frowns are polite everywhere.
Words are less useful than gestures.
Scientists reject the study of emotion.
qs.why: 표정은 보편적이고 손짓은 지역적이라는 대비가 중심이에요.

qs.q: Why does the writer say it is easy to forget that gestures are learned?
o: They are taught only in schools and in language classes.
They change every day.
They are printed in guidebooks.
They feel natural to the people who use them.
qs.why: gestures feel natural to the person who makes them.

qs.q: What advice does the writer give to unsure travelers?
o: Use as many gestures as possible.
Use words and a friendly face rather than uncertain gestures.
Avoid speaking in public.
Copy the gestures of their home country wherever they travel abroad.
qs.why: rely more on words, a calm voice, and a friendly face.

qs.q: What does the final sentence suggest the distinction can help us understand?
o: Only the differences between countries and their governments
Both shared humanity and cultural differences
Only the similarities among families
Why scientists dislike travelers
qs.why: common humanity and our differences.

items.title: Family Name First
items.text: When you write your name on an international form, you may hesitate. Which name comes first? In many English-speaking countries, the given name is placed before the family name, so a person called Maria Lopez uses Maria as the personal name. In Korea, Japan, and Hungary, among other places, the family name usually comes first. This difference can cause confusion in schools, airports, and on websites that assume only one order. Some people solve the problem by writing the family name in capital letters, so that the reader knows which part is which. Others simply explain politely when they introduce themselves. The question may seem small, but names are closely tied to identity, and getting them right is a simple way to show respect to someone from another culture.

qs.q: What is the main point of the passage?
o: Family names are unnecessary in modern life.
Only Korean people use family names first.
Capital letters are required on all official forms in every country.
Name order differs by culture and should be handled with care.
qs.why: 이름 순서가 문화마다 다르고 존중해야 한다는 내용이에요.

qs.q: According to the passage, how do some people avoid confusion?
o: By writing the family name in capital letters
By inventing a completely new name for use abroad
By using only initials
By refusing to fill in the form
qs.why: writing the family name in capital letters.

qs.q: Which of the following countries is NOT mentioned as placing the family name first?
o: Korea
Japan
Spain
Hungary
qs.why: Spain은 지문에 나오지 않아요.

qs.q: Why does the writer say that getting names right is important?
o: Names are easy to forget.
Forms are checked by the police at every airport.
Airports have strict rules.
Names are connected to a person's identity.
qs.why: names are closely tied to identity.

items.title: Thanks for the Harvest
items.text: In every season, a farmer's work depends on the earth, and many communities have created festivals to give thanks when the crops have been gathered. In Korea, families enjoy rice cakes and visit the places where their ancestors rest. In North America, a large autumn meal brings relatives together. Other regions hold lively markets with dancing and music. The details differ, but the festivals share a common purpose: to appreciate the effort of the year and to strengthen bonds among relatives and neighbors. Even in modern cities, where few people grow crops, such festivals remain popular because they offer a chance to slow down. Comparing harvest celebrations around the world helps students notice how different customs can grow from the same basic human feeling of gratitude.

qs.q: What do harvest festivals have in common?
o: They use exactly the same kind of food in every place.
They express gratitude and bring people together.
They are held only in farming villages.
They require special clothes.
qs.why: a common purpose: to appreciate the effort of the year and to strengthen bonds.

qs.q: Why do harvest festivals remain popular in modern cities?
o: They give people a chance to slow down.
Everyone in cities grows crops.
The festivals are very short.
City markets close during the festivals.
qs.why: they offer a chance to slow down.

qs.q: The passage mentions all of the following EXCEPT
o: rice cakes
a large autumn meal
a parade of animals
markets with dancing and music
qs.why: 동물 퍼레이드는 언급되지 않았어요.

qs.q: What is the purpose of the final sentence?
o: To explain the value of comparing different celebrations
To criticize modern cities for their fast and crowded way of life
To list the foods eaten at festivals
To advise students to avoid festivals
qs.why: 비교하면 다른 관습이 같은 감정에서 자란다는 것을 알 수 있다고 해요.

items.title: Reading Between the Messages
items.text: Online messages travel in a second, but their meaning can take much longer to understand. In some communities, people prefer to say exactly what they mean: a request is stated clearly, and a short reply is considered efficient. In others, speakers soften what they say, leaving the listener to read the situation, and a blunt message may seem rude. A reply of "maybe" might therefore be a polite way of saying no. Emojis add another layer, since a smile may show warmth in one chat and sarcasm in another. People who work on international teams often agree on simple rules, such as confirming key points in writing and asking for clarification without embarrassment. Such habits do not remove cultural differences, but they prevent small misunderstandings from growing into large ones.

qs.q: What does the writer suggest a reply of "maybe" might mean?
o: A promise to answer immediately
A request for more money from the sender
A polite refusal in some communities
A message sent by mistake
qs.why: a reply of 'maybe' might therefore be a polite way of saying no.

qs.q: What do international teams often do to avoid misunderstandings?
o: Stop using emojis altogether
Agree on simple communication rules
Write only very long and detailed messages
Avoid asking any questions
qs.why: agree on simple rules, such as confirming key points in writing.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
o: Emojis are more reliable than words.
Short replies are always rude.
Teams should work in separate rooms and offices to avoid conflict.
Cultural differences affect how online messages are understood.
qs.why: 온라인 메시지의 의미 해석이 문화에 따라 다르다는 내용이에요.

qs.q: The word "blunt" is closest in meaning to
o: very quiet
very slow
very direct
very friendly
qs.why: blunt는 '퉁명스러울 만큼 직설적인'이라는 뜻이에요.

qs.q: What does the final sentence suggest about the habits described?
o: They reduce the effect of differences without erasing them.
They make all cultures become exactly the same over a long time.
They are useless for small teams.
They are needed only for face-to-face talk.
qs.why: do not remove cultural differences, but they prevent small misunderstandings.

items.title: Cooking Together
items.text: Every year, as winter approaches, many Korean families gather to make large amounts of kimchi. This activity, known as kimjang, is more than food preparation. Neighbors and relatives exchange labor, share their recipes, and send jars to those who cannot cook for themselves. The tradition has been recognized by an international organization as part of humanity's intangible heritage, meaning a living practice rather than a building or object. Such heritage depends on people rather than stone. If young people stop learning the skills, the practice may fade even if the recipes are written down. That is why museums, schools, and community groups often invite children to take part. Preserving a custom, they argue, means keeping it alive in daily life rather than placing it behind glass.

qs.q: What does "intangible heritage" mean in the passage?
o: A building that cannot be visited
A recipe stored in a museum
A rare old tool that is owned by only one family in a village
A living practice rather than an object or building
qs.why: a living practice rather than a building or object.

qs.q: According to the passage, how is kimjang more than food preparation?
o: It is a cooking contest among the best chefs of the region.
It involves sharing work and caring for neighbors.
It is a sport played in winter.
It is a lesson taught only in schools.
qs.why: Neighbors and relatives exchange labor, share their recipes, and send jars.

qs.q: Why do community groups invite children to take part?
o: To reduce the cost of food for every family
To keep the custom alive in daily life
To avoid writing recipes
To protect old buildings
qs.why: Preserving a custom means keeping it alive in daily life.

qs.q: What can be inferred about heritage that depends on people?
o: It is safe once it has been written down.
It is protected by museum glass.
It never changes, even without any new learners.
It can fade if younger people do not learn it.
qs.why: If young people stop learning the skills, the practice may fade.

items.title: A Dinner with the Host Family
items.text:
Hana: Thank you for inviting me, Mrs. Brown. Dinner smells wonderful.
Mrs. Brown: You're welcome, Hana. Please help yourself. Do you eat everything?
Hana: Almost everything. At home, we usually say "I will eat well" before a meal, and I feel a little strange starting without saying it.
Mrs. Brown: That sounds lovely. Here we often just say "enjoy," but please say it your way.
Hana: May I ask something? In my country it is polite to finish all the rice. Is that the same here?
Mrs. Brown: Not exactly. Leaving a little on the plate is perfectly fine, and nobody will think you are rude.
Hana: Oh, that is a relief. I was worried that I would have to eat everything.
Mrs. Brown: Not at all. If you want more, just ask, and if you're full, a simple "no, thank you" is enough.
Hana: Then I'll try a little more of the potatoes. They are delicious!
Mrs. Brown: I'm glad. Tomorrow I'd love to hear about the meals you cook at home.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the conversation?
o: To compare table manners in two cultures
To plan a long trip to a restaurant in town
To explain how to cook potatoes
To complain about a late dinner
qs.why: 두 문화의 식사 예절을 비교하는 대화예요.

qs.q: What does Hana feel strange about at the start of the meal?
o: Sitting on a different kind of chair
Using a knife and fork for the first time at a table
Beginning to eat without a customary phrase
Being served before the host
qs.why: she feels a little strange starting without saying her phrase.

qs.q: What does Mrs. Brown say about leaving food on the plate?
o: It is considered impolite.
It means the cook should be thanked.
It is a sign of being hungry.
It is perfectly acceptable.
qs.why: Leaving a little on the plate is perfectly fine.

qs.q: Why does Hana say "that is a relief"?
o: She has just finished her dinner.
She no longer has to worry about finishing everything.
She has found the potatoes far too spicy to enjoy at dinner.
She learned that the meal is free.
qs.why: 접시를 다 비워야 한다는 걱정이 사라졌어요.

qs.q: What will Mrs. Brown probably do tomorrow?
o: Ask Hana about meals from her country
Teach Hana how to say a new phrase in English
Cook rice for the whole family
Take Hana to a market
qs.why: Tomorrow I'd love to hear about the meals you cook at home.

items.title: Preparing a Presentation
items.text:
Jin: Our topic is a local festival, but I don't know how to begin.
Sara: Let's start with something visual. We can show two photos, one from the parade and one from the market.
Jin: Good idea. But I'm afraid the audience will only see the colors and the food.
Sara: That is exactly the problem. The iceberg idea in our textbook says those are only the visible parts.
Jin: Then we should also explain the hidden part, like why people gather and what the festival means to them.
Sara: Right. I can interview my grandmother. She has joined the festival every year for more than fifty years.
Jin: Great. I'll look for some written sources, and I'll check that the information is correct.
Sara: We should also credit every photo and quote. That's part of being honest with other people's work.
Jin: Agreed. Shall we meet again on Friday to put the slides together?
Sara: Perfect. I'll bring the interview notes.

qs.q: Why are the speakers worried about showing only photos?
o: The photos are too small for the audience to see clearly in the hall.
The festival has no meaning at all.
The audience may notice only the surface of the festival.
The teacher dislikes visual material.
qs.why: 색과 음식만 보게 될까 봐 걱정해요.

qs.q: What does Sara plan to do?
o: Interview a family member
Visit a museum abroad
Buy tickets for the parade
Design a new festival
qs.why: I can interview my grandmother.

qs.q: What does Sara mean by "credit every photo and quote"?
o: Pay money for each item
Keep the sources secret

items.title: Does Yes Mean Yes?
items.text:
Ken: I asked Mr. Sato if he could join our team meeting, and he said, "That might be difficult."
Emma: That sounds like a no to me. Maybe he is just too busy.
Ken: But he didn't say no. I thought he might still come.
Emma: In some cultures, people avoid a direct refusal because it could hurt the other person's feelings.
Ken: So "difficult" could actually mean "I can't"?
Emma: Quite possibly. In my family, we would say the same thing to a polite neighbor.
Ken: Then I should ask a question that is easier to answer, such as which day would be convenient.
Emma: Exactly. That way he can suggest another time without feeling uncomfortable.
Ken: I see. I always thought being clear meant being direct.
Emma: Being clear can mean different things. Sometimes it means being kind and careful.

qs.q: What does Emma think Mr. Sato's answer means?
o: He will definitely come.
He wants to change the topic.
He probably cannot attend.
He has not heard the question.
qs.why: That sounds like a no to me.

qs.q: Why do some people avoid a direct refusal, according to Emma?
o: It might hurt the other person's feelings.
It takes too much time to say in a busy meeting.
It is against a school rule.
It makes meetings shorter.
qs.why: because it could hurt the other person's feelings.

qs.q: What does Ken decide to do next?
o: Cancel the meeting
Ask Mr. Sato to apologize
Send a longer message with many questions
Ask which day would be convenient
qs.why: ask a question that is easier to answer.

qs.q: What does Emma suggest about being clear?
o: It always means speaking loudly.
It can include being kind and careful.
It is never possible between cultures.
It means avoiding all questions.
qs.why: Sometimes it means being kind and careful.

qs.q: The phrase "a direct refusal" in the conversation means
o: asking for a delay
saying no plainly
making a joke
writing a long reply
qs.why: direct refusal은 분명하게 거절하는 것을 뜻해요.

items.title: Two Kinds of English
items.text:
Lucy: I'm confused. My cousin from London told me to take the lift, but I couldn't find any lifts.
Daniel: In American English we say elevator. Lift is the British word.
Lucy: And she also said she lives in a flat. I thought she meant a flat tire!
Daniel: Ha! In British English, a flat is an apartment. There are many pairs like that.
Lucy: Is one of them correct and the other one wrong?
Daniel: No. Both are standard, and they simply belong to different regions.
Lucy: Then which one should I use in my English class in Korea?
Daniel: Either is fine, but try to stay consistent in one piece of writing, and learn to recognize the other.
Lucy: That makes sense. Being able to understand both seems more useful than choosing a winner.
Daniel: Exactly. English belongs to everyone who uses it.

qs.q: Why was Lucy confused?
o: She had never ridden in an elevator.
Her cousin spoke a different language.
She could not find London.
She did not know a British word.
qs.why: lift라는 영국식 단어를 몰라 헷갈렸어요.

qs.q: What does Daniel say about British and American words?
o: Both are standard in their own regions.
British words are older, better, and more correct.
American words are wrong in school.
Only one of them is used in Korea.
qs.why: Both are standard.

qs.q: What advice does Daniel give about writing?
o: Switch varieties in every sentence
Avoid using any British words
Be consistent within one text
Write only in the spoken style
qs.why: try to stay consistent in one piece of writing.

qs.q: Which statement would Daniel most likely agree with?
o: English belongs only to its native speakers.
A single variety should replace all the others.
Regional words are not worth learning.
Understanding several varieties is valuable.
qs.why: English belongs to everyone who uses it.

items.q: In a culture where much of the meaning is understood from the situation and not stated in words, communication is called ____.

items.q: Choose the best word. The city is famous for its cultural ____, with people from many backgrounds living together.

devotion

items.good: Although the two cultures differ in many ways, they share some basic values.
items.ko: 두 문화는 여러 면에서 다르지만 몇 가지 기본 가치를 공유해요.
bad: Although the two cultures differ in many ways, but they share some basic values.
Despite the two cultures differ in many ways, they share some basic values.
Although differ the two cultures in many ways, they share some basic values.

items.rule: Although는 절을 이끄는 접속사이고, 주절 앞에 but을 함께 쓰지 않아요. Despite는 뒤에 명사(구)가 와요.
items.hint: 접속사 뒤에는 주어와 동사가 오는지 생각해 보세요.

items.good: Many English words have been borrowed from other languages.

bad: Many English words have borrowed from other languages.
Many English words has been borrowed from other languages.
Many English words are been borrowed from other languages.

items.rule: 복수 주어와 수동태 현재완료는 have been + 과거분사로 써요.

items.good: The festival, which takes place every autumn, attracts visitors from around the world.
items.ko: 그 축제는 매년 가을에 열리며 전 세계에서 방문객을 끌어들여요.

items.rule: 쉼표가 있는 계속적 용법의 관계대명사로는 that을 쓸 수 없고, 사물 선행사에는 which를 써요. 관계사절에서는 대명사 it을 반복하지 않아요.

If I live abroad, I would try to learn the local language.

items.rule: 현재 사실과 반대되는 가정은 If + 과거형, 주어 + would + 동사원형으로 나타내요.

items.rule: look forward to의 to는 전치사라서 뒤에 동명사(-ing)가 와요.

items.good: Not only does the festival celebrate music, but it also showcases local food.

bad: Not only the festival celebrates music, but it also showcases local food.
Not only does the festival celebrates music, but it also showcases local food.
Not only the festival does celebrate music, but it also showcases local food.

items.rule: Not only가 문장 앞에 오면 주어와 조동사가 도치되고(does + 주어 + 동사원형), 동사는 원형이 돼요.

items.good: The guide said that the castle had been built over five hundred years ago.

bad: The guide said that the castle has been built over five hundred years ago.
The guide said that the castle is built over five hundred years ago.
The guide said that the castle had built over five hundred years ago.

items.rule: 전달 동사가 과거이고 그보다 앞선 일을 수동으로 말할 때는 had been + 과거분사를 써요. ago는 현재완료와 함께 쓰지 않아요.

items.good: The more we learn about other cultures, the less we rely on stereotypes.
items.ko: 다른 문화에 대해 더 많이 배울수록 고정관념에 덜 의존하게 돼요.
bad: The more we learn about other cultures, the lesser we rely on stereotypes.
More we learn about other cultures, less we rely on stereotypes.
The most we learn about other cultures, the least we rely on stereotypes.

cz.st: The more we learn about other cultures, the ___ we rely on stereotypes.

items.rule: the + 비교급 ~, the + 비교급 ...은 '~할수록 더 ...하다'라는 구문이에요. 동사 rely를 꾸미는 부사는 less예요.
